newsitem.title: USA: Senator D'Amato introduces U.S. bank reform bill.
newsitem.headline: Senator D'Amato introduces U.S. bank reform bill.

text.p: Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato weighed into the heated debate over bank reform on Tuesday, introducing a bill that would permit financial companies to combine with non-financial companies.
As expected, D'Amato's bill would tear down laws enacted after the Depression that separated banking from other financial services such as insurance and securities underwriting.
"This banking reform legislation will reform the current patchwork of laws and allow the market to operate freely within the financial services industry," the New York Republican said in a statement.

While most in Congress and the industry agree that the separation between banks and other financial services should be torn down, there is little consensus over measures like D'Amato's that would go even farther.

At a House Banking subcommittee hearing on Tuesday, representatives of the thrift, insurance and mutual fund industries said they favored unfettered combinations of financial and non-financial companies. That could allow, for example, Ford Motor Co or Microsoft Corp to own or be owned by Citicorp or Aetna Inc.
But small banks and consumer groups, along with House Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach, oppose permitting such combinations.
"Our laws must be updated to reflect modern times, where non-bank firms such as cable and software companies are designing and delivering bank-like services over the Internet," D'Amato said.

To protect the federal deposit insurance system from the risks posed by the failure of large, diversified company, D'Amato's bill proposes that financial services companies be organized under a holding company structure.
In theory, if a non-bank subsidiary of a holding company failed, the subsidiary containing federally insured bank deposits would not be affected.

The bill would prohibit a depository institution from engaging in certain currently permissable activities involving securities, insurance and real estate. Dealing and underwriting in securities, underwriting insurance and investing in and developing real estate would all have to be done by another subsidiary under the holding company.
Employees of a depository institution would be permitted to market such services provided by an affiliated subsidiary.

Also, a holding company would have to purchase an existing insurance agency or real estate brokerage firm to enter those businesses. It would not be permitted to start its own from scratch for at least five years after the bill became law.

D'Amato also proposed that each line of business be regulated by an "appropriate" federal regulator, an approach known as "functional regulation." For example, the Securities and Exchange Commission, which currently oversees the activities of securities firms, would regulate securities activities of any holding company affiliate.
Some legislative initiatives have proposed making the Federal Reserve the primary regulator of financial companies at the holding company level.

D'Amato would not elevate any exisiting regulator to oversee holding companies, but would create a body called the "National Financial Oversight Committee" comprised of represenatives of all federal agencies responsible for regulating financial institutions. State regulators would also be permitted to participate in the committee's deliberations.
The bill would also bar states from enacting laws that discriminate against holding companies or their affiliates.

"Whether couched as affiliation, licensing or agency restrictions or as constraints on access to state courts, such laws effectively perpetuate market barriers and deny consumers the opportunity to choose," a summary of D'Amato's bill handed out by his office said.
